mainTopic: The oath when two hold a טלית, holding back disputed money, and the oath when witnesses prove part of a claim
overview: The גמרא finishes a קל וחומר showing that סומכוס should not require a שבועה when two people hold a טלית. It answers that the שבועה is only a rabbinic safeguard, as רבי יוחנן explains, so that people will not grab others' garments. Next the גמרא asks whether our משנה fits רבי יוסי or רבנן, who put disputed money aside until אליהו comes in the case of two depositors. It answers that in the depositors' case someone is surely lying, but with the טלית both may have picked it up together. A second answer, about pressuring a cheater to confess, is rejected because it does not fit the buying case. The גמרא then explains the storekeeper case, where both sides swear and collect from the homeowner, because each has his own claim against him. Finally, רבי חייא teaches that when witnesses prove part of a claim, the defendant must swear on the rest. Our משנה supports this, and רבה's reason for the oath of מודה מקצת הטענה begins; it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the argument that סומכוס would not require an oath
steps.stepSummary: In סומכוס's case the doubt is real, since each side might own all of it, and still they split without a שבועה. In our case it might truly belong to both, so all the more so there should be no oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it could be that it all belongs to one, and it could be that it all belongs to the other. Even so, סומכוס says: money in doubt is split without an oath. Here there is no real money-doubt, because it may really belong to both of them. Isn't it obvious that they should split without an oath?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a challenge that began just before this point. It argues that our משנה, which requires a שבועה, cannot match סומכוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a קל וחומר. In סומכוס's case one person really owns everything, so splitting will surely give someone what is not his, and still he says no oath is needed. In our case both people may each truly own half, so the case for splitting without an oath is even stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: Money whose owner is in doubt
They split it without taking an oath
A real financial doubt, where each side might own all of it
All the more so (a קל וחומר)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't get mixed up here: a case WITH דררא דממונא is the harder case for splitting. The גמרא says that if סומכוס lets them split without an oath there, then here, with no such doubt, there is even more reason to split without one.

phrases.english: and it is possible to say it all belongs to this one,
and it is possible to say it all belongs to that one,
and still Sumakhos says:
money whose ownership is in doubt
they divide without an oath,
here, where there is no real financial doubt,
since one can say it belongs to both of them,
is it not all the more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא, דְּלֵיכָּא דְּרָרָא דְמָמוֹנָא, דְּאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר דְּתַרְוַיְיהוּ הִיא, לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a challenge begun before this section, against the claim that our משנה could follow סומכוס.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that our משנה, which requires a שבועה, can follow סומכוס.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר: if סומכוס drops the oath where only one side truly owns it, he should surely drop it where both may own it.

steps.title: The oath is only a rabbinic safeguard
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה can follow סומכוס. The שבועה is not required by the basic law. It is a rabbinic enactment, explained by רבי יוחנן, to stop people from grabbing others' garments.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say our משנה follows סומכוס. This oath is only rabbinic, as רבי יוחנן said: this oath is an enactment of the Sages, so that people will not grab someone else's טלית and say, 'It's mine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. סומכוס is right that by basic law they split without an oath, but the Sages added this שבועה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed the oath comes from the basic money law. The answer moves the oath to a different level: it is a rabbinic protection against grabbing. So סומכוס's rule about basic law does not clash with it.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say (the משנה follows this opinion)
Required by the Rabbis, not by the Torah
An enactment made by the Sages

steps.whatToRemember: The שבועה in our משנה is a rabbinic enactment (רבי יוחנן) to stop people from grabbing what isn't theirs. That is why it fits even סומכוס.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבי יוחנן's explanation of this oath as a תקנת חכמים is the basic way to understand the שבועה of our משנה.

phrases.english: You may even say it follows Sumakhos:
this oath is from the Rabbis
like Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
For Rabbi Yochanan said:
this oath is an enactment of the Sages,
so that not everyone
will go and grab hold of his friend's garment
and say: It is mine.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא סוֹמְכוֹס, שְׁבוּעָה זוֹ מִדְּרַבָּנַן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קל וחומר of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different level of law: the oath is rabbinic, not part of the basic money law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The שבועה was thought to be part of the basic law of dividing, which would clash with סומכוס.
steps.terutzMaskana: The שבועה is a rabbinic safeguard against grabbing, so סומכוס can agree with the משנה.

steps.title: Does our משנה disagree with רבי יוסי?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says that in a doubtful case nothing should be handed out, so that a cheater gains nothing; everything waits until אליהו comes. Our משנה splits the טלית, so it seems not to follow him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say our משנה does not follow רבי יוסי? If it did, he said: 'If so, what did the cheater lose? Rather, everything should be put aside until אליהו comes.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. It suggests that our משנה goes against רבי יוסי's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי wants the cheater to lose by having the whole item held back. Our משנה gives each person half, so a liar still walks away with something. That seems to be against רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (a suggestion the גמרא tests)
Until אליהו comes and settles the doubt

phrases.english: Shall we say our Mishnah is not like Rabbi Yosei?
For if it were like Rabbi Yosei,
doesn't he say:
If so, what did the cheater lose?
phrases.notes: He says this later (דף לז.) about two people who left 100 and 200 with one keeper, who forgot whose was which.

phrases.english: Rather, everything should be put aside
until Elijah comes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new line, testing the משנה against a different תנא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of our משנה that the two holders split the טלית.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי holds back everything so the cheater gains nothing; splitting lets a cheater gain.

steps.title: Even רבנן seem to disagree with our משנה
steps.stepSummary: Even רבנן, who disagree with רבי יוסי, put aside the disputed part until אליהו comes. The whole טלית is in doubt, just like that disputed part, so even רבנן should hold it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what, then, will you say, that it follows רבנן? Since רבנן say 'the rest is put aside until אליהו comes,' this case is just like 'the rest,' because it is in doubt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: blaming only רבי יוסי does not help. רבנן also seem to clash with our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even רבנן hand out only the amount each person surely owns. The amount in doubt is held back. Here the whole טלית is in doubt, so by רבנן's logic it should also be held, and the problem now seems to apply to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: But what then? (pushing back on a suggestion)
The remainder, the part in doubt

steps.confusionAlert: רבנן do not hold back everything. They give each person the amount he surely owns and hold back only the doubtful extra. The גמרא's point is that the whole טלית counts as 'doubtful extra.'

phrases.english: But what, then? Like the Rabbis?
Since the Rabbis say:
"The remainder is put aside
until Elijah comes,"
this case too is like the remainder,
since it is a doubt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the narrow suggestion of step 3 and widens the difficulty to רבנן as well.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that our משנה could at least match רבנן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבנן hold back any doubtful amount; the whole טלית is doubtful, so it too should be held.

steps.title: Why רבנן hold back the depositors' money but split the טלית
steps.stepSummary: In the depositors' case the disputed מנה surely belongs to only one person, so רבנן hold it back. Our טלית might belong to both, so רבנן let them split it with a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What kind of comparison is this? It works fine if you say our משנה follows רבנן. There, the disputed מנה surely belongs to just one of them, so רבנן say to put it aside until אליהו comes. Here, it is possible the טלית belongs to both, so רבנן say they split it with an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the comparison from Step 4. The case of the depositors is different from our case of the טלית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the depositors' case, splitting the disputed מנה would surely give half of it to the wrong person, because it belongs to only one of them. With the טלית, both people may really own it together, so splitting could be exactly right. That is why רבנן can hold the money back there and still split the טלית here.

keyTerms.meaning: What is this? (This comparison doesn't work.)
A sum of one hundred זוז
It should be put aside until אליהו comes

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key idea of the whole section. Splitting is a fair outcome only when each side might truly own a share.

phrases.english: What is this comparison?
It works out fine if you say it follows the Rabbis:
There, where this hundred certainly
belongs to one of them,
the Rabbis say: it should be put aside
until Elijah comes.
Here, where one can say that it belongs to both of them,
the Rabbis say: they divide it with an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי מַאי? אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבנן in Step 4
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (אוקימתא of the facts)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole טלית is in doubt just like the disputed מנה, so רבנן should hold it back too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The disputed מנה surely belongs to only one person. The טלית may belong to both, so splitting it is fair.

steps.title: רבי יוסי should hold back the טלית all the more
steps.stepSummary: If רבי יוסי holds back even the money that surely belongs to each depositor, then all the more he would hold back a טלית that might belong entirely to one person.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if you say our משנה follows רבי יוסי, there is a problem. There, each person surely owns at least a מנה, and still רבי יוסי says to put everything aside until אליהו comes. Here, where it may all belong to just one of them, all the more so it should be put aside!
steps.whatsHappening: Still continuing the same answer, the גמרא admits that רבי יוסי remains a problem. It backs this up with a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the depositors' case each side surely owns at least one מנה, yet רבי יוסי still holds back everything. In our case one person might own nothing at all. So holding back the טלית should be even more obvious, and our משנה, which splits it, seems not to follow רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, if even... (opens a קל וחומר)

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי אָמְרַתְּ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הִיא,
phrases.english: But if you say it follows Rabbi Yosei,
now, if there,
where there is certainly a hundred for this one
and a hundred for that one,
Rabbi Yosei says it should all be put aside
until Elijah comes,

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא דְּאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר דְּחַד מִינַּיְיהוּ הוּא –
phrases.english: here, where one can say it belongs to just one of them,
all the more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִי אָמְרַתְּ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the בשלמא/אלא structure. Rescues רבנן but presses the problem from רבי יוסי (Step 3) with a קל וחומר, which Step 7 then answers.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that our משנה could follow רבי יוסי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר: if he holds back money that each side surely partly owns, he should surely hold back a טלית that one side may not own at all.

steps.title: Even רבי יוסי: here there may be no cheater
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי holds the money back only because there is surely a cheater. With the טלית, both may have picked it up at the same time, so maybe nobody is lying.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say our משנה follows רבי יוסי. There, there is surely a cheater. Here, who says anyone is cheating? Maybe both of them picked up the טלית together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against Step 6 and shows that our משנה can follow רבי יוסי after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי's rule is aimed at a case where someone is surely lying. With the depositors, one of them must be lying about the extra מנה. With the טלית, both may honestly have lifted it at once, so there is no cheater to work against.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows Rabbi Yosei:
there, there is certainly a cheater;
here, who says there is a cheater?
Say that both of them picked it up at the same time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קל וחומר from Step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (certain cheater vs. possible honest claims)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוסי holds back anything that is in doubt, so all the more he would hold back the טלית.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוסי holds things back only when someone is surely lying. With the טלית, both may be honest.

steps.title: Second answer: holding back the טלית would not make a cheater confess
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי penalizes the cheating depositor so that he will confess and get back his own real money. With the טלית, a cheater loses nothing by having it held back, so he has no reason to confess.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or another answer: there, רבי יוסי penalizes the cheater so that he will admit the truth. Here, what does a cheater lose that would make him admit the truth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different reason why רבי יוסי could agree with our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the depositors' case, holding everything back also locks up the cheater's own real מנה, so he has a reason to confess and get it back. In the טלית case a cheater put nothing of his own in, so holding the טלית back costs him nothing. The penalty would not achieve its goal here.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוסי's 'put it aside until אליהו comes' is a penalty against a cheater. Our משנה can still follow him: in the טלית case there may be no cheater (Step 7), and holding it back would not push a cheater to confess (Step 8).

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי: הָתָם קָנֵיס לֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי לְרַמַּאי
phrases.english: Alternatively: there, Rabbi Yosei penalizes the cheater
so that he will admit the truth,

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא מַאי פְּסֵידָא אִית לֵיהּ דְּלוֹדֵי.
phrases.english: here, what loss does he have that would make him admit?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי: הָתָם קָנֵיס לֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי לְרַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to Step 6, alongside Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the purpose of the rule (it is a penalty meant to make a cheater confess)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Holding things back is simply what you do whenever ownership is unclear.
steps.terutzMaskana: Holding things back is a penalty that pushes a cheater to confess. It would do nothing with the טלית, where a cheater has nothing of his own to lose.

steps.title: The second answer only works for a found item
steps.stepSummary: The answer from Step 8 fits a מציאה, but it does not fit the case of מקח וממכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for a found item. But for buying and selling, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the answer given in Step 8. It shows that the answer cannot explain the buying case in our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said a cheater over a found טלית loses nothing if it is held back, so pressuring him would not get him to confess. That is true for a מציאה, because he paid nothing for it. But in מקח וממכר each side claims he paid money, so a cheater would lose something real, and holding it back could pressure him.

keyTerms.meaning: It works out fine (for this case)
What is there to say? (this answer does not fit)

phrases.english: This works well for a found item;
but buying and selling,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּינַח מְצִיאָה, מִקָּח וּמִמְכָּר מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 8
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the Step 8 answer, which was based on pressuring the cheater to confess
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It explains a found item but not a purchase, where the cheater did pay money and could be pressured

steps.title: Back to the first answer
steps.stepSummary: Since the second answer fails, the גמרא goes back to the answer from Step 7: with the טלית, maybe nobody is lying.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is clear that the answer is as we explained at first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles on the first answer it gave in Step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי holds money back only when someone is surely a cheater. In our משנה, both people may truly have grabbed the טלית together, or both may have paid for it, so no one is surely lying. That answer works for both the found case and the buying case.
steps.whatToRemember: The difference between our טלית and רבי יוסי's depositors: in the depositors' case someone is surely lying, but with the טלית maybe nobody is.

phrases.english: Rather, it is clear
as we answered at first.
phrases.notes: He means the answer from before: in our case maybe nobody is lying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting Step 8, returns to Step 7
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יוסי holds money back only where there is surely a cheater. In our משנה that is not certain, so the טלית is divided.

steps.title: The storekeeper case: someone is surely lying, yet nothing is held back
steps.stepSummary: In the חנווני על פנקסו case, both sides swear and get paid. Why don't we take the money from the homeowner and put it aside until אליהו comes, since someone is surely lying?
steps.simpleTranslation: Both according to the רבנן and according to רבי יוסי, there is the case of a storekeeper relying on his ledger, where the משנה teaches: this one swears and takes, and that one swears and takes. What is different there, that we do not say: take the money out from the homeowner and let it rest until אליהו comes? After all, there is certainly a cheater!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a case from another משנה that seems to clash with the rule it just settled on. There someone is surely lying, yet the money is not held back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said that money is held back when there is surely a cheater. In the storekeeper case, either the storekeeper or the worker must be lying, because the food was either given or not. Yet both swear and the homeowner pays both, which goes against that rule. Even the רבנן hold back the disputed part when only one person can be right, so this is a problem for both opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: A storekeeper relying on his account book

steps.confusionAlert: Both the storekeeper and the worker collect from the homeowner. The worker does not collect from the storekeeper. The homeowner ends up paying twice.

phrases.english: Both according to the Rabbis and according to Rabbi Yosei,
there, regarding a storekeeper relying on his ledger,
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in שבועות: the employer told the storekeeper to give food to his worker, and now they argue about whether it was given.

phrases.english: which teaches:
this one swears and takes,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the storekeeper, and "that one" in the next line is the worker.

phrases.english: and that one swears and takes.
What is different, that we do not say:
take the money out from the homeowner,
and let it rest until Eliyahu comes,
since there is certainly a cheater!

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּין לְרַבָּנַן וּבֵין לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, הָתָם גַּבֵּי חֶנְוָנִי עַל פִּנְקָסוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the rule settled in Step 10 against another משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in the storekeeper משנה, which lets both sides collect, according to both רבנן and רבי יוסי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: When someone is surely lying, money is held back until אליהו comes. In the storekeeper case someone is surely lying, so the money should be held back instead of being paid to both.

steps.title: The storekeeper says: I did your errand, so you pay me
steps.stepSummary: The storekeeper has a claim on the homeowner himself. The homeowner sent him and trusted the worker without witnesses, so the homeowner cannot push him off.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: There, this is the reason. The storekeeper can say to the homeowner: "I was doing your errand. What do I have to do with the worker? Even if he swears to me, I do not believe him with his oath. You are the one who trusted him, since you did not tell me: Give it to him in front of witnesses."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing that the storekeeper case is different. The storekeeper's claim is against the homeowner, not against the worker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding money back fits a case where two people fight over one sum of money. Here the storekeeper acted as the homeowner's שליח, so his claim is on the homeowner alone. The homeowner caused the doubt by not asking for witnesses, so he must pay the storekeeper, and the worker's oath cannot block that payment.

keyTerms.meaning: An errand done for someone else, agency

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that holding money back is for two people fighting over the same money. It does not apply when each side has his own separate claim against the payer.

phrases.english: They say: There,
this is the reason:
because the storekeeper says to the homeowner:
I was doing your errand,
what do I have to do with the hired worker?

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּקָא מִשְׁתְּבַע לִי,
phrases.english: Even though he swears to me,
he is not believed by me with an oath.
You are the one who trusted him,
since you did not tell me:
"Give it to him in front of witnesses."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי הָתָם, הַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ חֶנְוָנִי לְבַעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: the storekeeper has his own claim against the homeowner
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The storekeeper case is like any doubt with a sure cheater, so the money should be held back
steps.terutzMaskana: The storekeeper acted as the homeowner's שליח and the homeowner trusted the worker without witnesses, so the homeowner must pay the storekeeper no matter what the worker swears

steps.title: The worker also has his own claim against the homeowner
steps.stepSummary: The worker tells the homeowner: I worked for you, and I have nothing to do with the storekeeper. His oath means nothing to me.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the worker can also say to the homeowner: I did work for you. What business do I have with the storekeeper? Even if he swears to me, I don't believe him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the answer from Step 12. Just like the storekeeper has a claim on the homeowner, the worker does too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker's deal was with the homeowner, not with the storekeeper. So the storekeeper's oath cannot cancel the worker's wages. Each side's claim stands on its own against the homeowner.

keyTerms.meaning: He is not trustworthy to me

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׂכִיר נָמֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ לְבַעַל הַבַּיִת:
phrases.english: And the worker also says to the homeowner:
I did the work for you;
what business do I have with the storekeeper?
Even though he swears to me,
phrases.notes: He means the storekeeper swearing that he already gave the worker his pay.

phrases.english: he is not believed by me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשָׂכִיר נָמֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ לְבַעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer of Step 12 by giving the worker's side.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each party has an independent claim against the homeowner
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since one of the two claimants must be lying, the homeowner should not have to pay both.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both the worker and the storekeeper have a direct claim on the homeowner, so neither can be pushed off.

steps.title: Both swear and both collect from the homeowner
steps.stepSummary: Because each has his own claim, both swear and both get paid by the homeowner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, both of them swear and take payment from the homeowner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the חנווני על פנקסו discussion. Both sides swear, and both are paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why we do not hold the money until אליהו comes, as both רבנן and רבי יוסי do in the depositors' case. The homeowner is truly obligated to each one, so it does not matter that one of them is lying to the other.
steps.whatToRemember: In the חנווני על פנקסו case, the homeowner pays both sides. He created both obligations himself, so even if one side is lying, the money is not held back the way it is in the depositors' case (by both רבנן and רבי יוסי).

phrases.english: Therefore, both of them swear
and take payment from the homeowner.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִלְכָּךְ, תַּרְוַיְיהוּ מִשְׁתַּבְעִי וְשָׁקְלִי מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical result from Steps 12-13.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both claimants swear and are paid by the homeowner, which answers the question of Step 11.

steps.title: Witnesses prove half the loan, so he pays half and swears on the rest
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא teaches: someone claims a מנה, and the other denies everything. Witnesses say he owes fifty זוז. He pays fifty and swears about the rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא taught: One says, 'You have a מנה of mine.' The other says, 'You have nothing with me.' Witnesses testify that he owes fifty זוז. He gives him fifty זוז and swears about the rest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא from רבי חייא. When witnesses prove part of a claim, the defendant pays that part and must swear about the remaining part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The defendant denied everything, but witnesses proved he owes half. Paying that half is not enough to end the case. He must also take an oath that he does not owe the other half.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred זוז
A coin, the same as a דינר

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya taught:
"I have a maneh in your hand,"
phrases.notes: A מנה is one hundred זוז, so the claim is for 100.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר: אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי כְּלוּם,
phrases.english: and the other says: "You have nothing at all in my hand,"
and the witnesses testify about him
that he has fifty zuz with him —
he gives him fifty zuz,
and swears about the rest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic, not connected to the חנווני discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When witnesses prove part of a claim, the defendant pays that part and swears about the remainder.

steps.title: The source: witnesses are stronger than his own admission
steps.stepSummary: The rule comes from a קל וחומר. A person's own admission of part of a claim obligates an oath, so witnesses should obligate one even more.
steps.simpleTranslation: For his own admission should not be stronger than the testimony of witnesses, by a קל וחומר.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains where רבי חייא's rule comes from: a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who admits to part of a claim (מודה במקצת) must swear about the rest. Witnesses are stronger proof than his own words. So when witnesses prove part of the claim, he surely has to swear about the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: A logical argument from a lighter case to a stronger one

steps.confusionAlert: The defendant here admitted nothing, so this is not the regular מודה במקצת case. The oath comes only because the קל וחומר compares the witnesses to an admission.

phrases.english: For the admission of his own mouth should not be
phrases.notes: This points to the rule that someone who admits part of a claim has to swear about the rest.

phrases.english: greater than the testimony of witnesses,
from a kal vachomer.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁלֹּא תְּהֵא הוֹדָאַת פִּיו גְּדוֹלָה מֵהַעֲדָאַת עֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the ruling in Step 15.
steps.raayaObject: The oath required when witnesses prove part of a claim
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from the oath of מודה במקצת

steps.title: Our משנה of the טלית teaches the same idea
steps.stepSummary: Two people hold a טלית, and each one's grip is like witnesses for the part he holds. Even so, the משנה says each must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: And our תנא taught it too: two people are holding a טלית, and each says, 'I found it.' Since each is holding it, it is as if we are witnesses that what each one holds is his. Yet the משנה teaches that he must swear!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that our משנה matches רבי חייא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding part of the טלית works like witnesses proving that part of each claim is true. The משנה still requires an oath for the rest. That is exactly רבי חייא's rule: partial proof by witnesses leads to an oath on the remainder.

keyTerms.meaning: Our תנא (the משנה) also taught it
We are witnesses, meaning it is obvious to all

steps.whyThisMatters: This links the opening משנה of the פרק to the rule of witnesses to part of a claim. It gives one possible reason why the people holding the טלית must swear.

phrases.english: And our Tanna also taught it:
Two are holding a garment,
this one says "I found it," etc.
And here, since each one is holding it,
we are witnesses
that what this one holds is his,
and what that one holds is his,
and yet it teaches: he swears!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for רבי חייא's rule from our משנה.
steps.raayaObject: רבי חייא's rule that witnesses to part of a claim obligate an oath
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of שנים אוחזין בטלית, where each one's grip acts like witnesses and an oath is still required

steps.title: Why was the comparison to witnesses needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the point is of רבי חייא's line that a person's own admission should not count for more than witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of saying, 'so that a person's own admission should not be stronger than witnesses, by a קל וחומר'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It asks why רבי חייא felt he had to spell out this קל וחומר at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 16, רבי חייא argued that if admitting part of a claim brings an oath, then witnesses proving part of it should bring an oath even more. The גמרא now asks why this needed saying, since it seems obvious. The answer will show that the comparison was not as simple as it looks.

keyTerms.meaning: The admission of his own mouth, when a person himself admits part of the claim
A 'how much more so' argument: if a rule applies in a weaker case, it applies even more in a stronger case

phrases.english: What is meant by: 'so that the admission of his own mouth should not be
greater than the testimony of witnesses, by a קל וחומר'?
phrases.notes: This quotes רבי חייא's reasoning from step 16.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״שֶׁלֹּא תְּהֵא הוֹדָאַת פִּיו גְּדוֹלָה מֵהַעֲדָאַת עֵדִים מִקַּל וָחוֹמֶר״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the קל וחומר of step 16 and asks why it had to be stated.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי חייא needed to state the קל וחומר from admission to witnesses explicitly.

steps.title: Without it, we might think only admission brings an oath
steps.stepSummary: The קל וחומר was needed so no one would think the oath applies only to a person's own admission, following רבה's reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that you should not say: only a person's own admission is what the Torah put an oath on, following the explanation of רבה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Without the קל וחומר, we might think the oath belongs only to the case where a person admits part of the claim himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that the oath for admitting part of a claim has a special reason, and that reason fits only a person's own admission, not witnesses. If that were true, witnesses would not lead to an oath. The גמרא points to רבה's explanation as the source of that special reason.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳

phrases.english: So that you should not say
that it is only the admission of his own mouth
that the Merciful One placed an oath upon
according to רבה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18's question about why the קל וחומר was needed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The קל וחומר blocks the idea that the oath is tied only to a person's own admission, because רבה gives a reason that seems to fit only admission.

steps.title: רבה: a borrower won't deny everything to his lender's face
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that the Torah requires an oath from one who admits part of a claim because a person does not have the nerve to deny the whole debt to his creditor's face.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבה said: Why did the Torah say that one who admits part of a claim must swear? Because there is a presumption that a person does not act brazenly in front of his creditor. This borrower really wants to deny the whole debt, and the only reason he did not deny all of it is that a person does not act brazenly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבה's reason for the oath of מודה מקצת הטענה. The passage ends in the middle of his explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה says the borrower would like to deny the whole debt, but he is too embarrassed to deny all of it to the face of the person who lent him money. His partial admission comes from that feeling. This reason is about the person's own behavior, which is why someone might think it does not apply when witnesses prove part of the debt.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits to part of the claim against him
A presumption about how people normally act
Acts brazenly or shamelessly, to someone's face
Creditor, the one who lent the money

steps.confusionAlert: רבה is not saying the borrower is honest. He is saying the borrower wanted to deny everything and held back only out of embarrassment. That is why the admission alone does not settle the case.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבה's reason is the classic explanation for why the Torah imposes this oath. It ties the oath to the borrower's own psychology, and that is exactly what makes the comparison to witnesses less obvious.

phrases.english: As רבה said:
For what reason did the Torah say
that one who admits part of the claim must swear?
There is a presumption: a person does not act brazenly
in front of his creditor,
and this one really wants to deny all of it,
and the fact that he did not deny all of it
is because a person does not act brazenly

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבָּה: מִפְּנֵי מָה אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה מוֹדֶה מִקְצָת הַטַּעֲנָה יִשָּׁבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the רבה reference made in step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah imposes an oath on one who admits part of a claim because a person is presumed too embarrassed to deny the whole debt to his creditor's face, even though he would like to.
